newsitem.title: USA: Toy designer sees work as neat and cool.
newsitem.headline: Toy designer sees work as neat and cool.

text.p: For most of us, work is a four letter word. If it was supposed to be fun, it would be called fun. But for Mary Rodas, who designed the popular toy Balzac, work and fun are interchangable.
Mary entered the world of work/fun officially at 14, when she designed the balloon filled ball. More than $100 million worth of Balzacs have sold.

Now, at 21, she's the vice president of marketing at Balzac's manufacturer Catco Inc. She's a full-time toy developer and tester and she's a full-time student at New York Univeristy. Her worlds don't collide, she said, they intersect perfectly.
She's constantly designing, testing or revamping toys, even when she's in a classroom, at a mall or in her New York office.
"This is fun, and everything," Rodas said. "I take something out of both worlds."
The uses the real world as her test marketer. "I ask classmates, my peers, for feedback. I also ask my younger sister," she said.
Being out and about keeps her mindful of what customers want. "They want what I want -- to get my whole money's worth and to be entertained."
Because she says she's not much older than "a kid," she knows that the secret to designing a good toy is to keep it simple. And what's more enjoyable and basic than a ball.

Enter Balzac -- the name originally was a combination of "ball" and "sack" -- a basic ball with a twist. First introduced in 1990, Balzac is a cloth covered sphere that houses an inflated balloon. It's designed so a child never has real contact with the balloon, for safety reasons, but has a balloon's bounce and unpredictablity.
Balzac, which has bred boutiques in major department and toy stores, now comes in 15 sizes and remains the biggest seller at Catco.
A new addition to the Balzac line will be introduced at the upcoming New York International Toy Fair, one of the premier trade gatherings for the toy industry.
Working with Dee Snider, former lead singer of the rock band Twisted Sister, Rodas has developed Horror Head Balls, laytex covered balloon balls with monster faces, aimed at an older audience.
They will be in stores this year and will sell for $7.99 to $20, depending on the size.
Mini Balzacs are also making their debut this year. The Micro Pro-Line toys are miniature versions and have adjustable weights.
She gives Micro Pros the "kid" seal of approval by deeming them "fun and everything."

Another basic toy is the water pistol, but Rodas feels that many adults don't like their children playing with anything that has a violent sub-text. That's how she came up with the new Spit Heads, which are shaped like puppets but act like water guns.
"It doesn't look violent, but kids still think of it as a water gun," she said. "It hides the violent content, but kids like it becuase they think it's funny."
She gives Spit Heads a very high rating -- "they're cool, they're neat."
Spit Heads will sell for about $15 and will come in three designs, the T-Rex dinosaur, blue alien and purple gargoyle.

The daughter of El Salvadoran immigrants, Rodas was "discovered" by Donald Spector, inventor and chairman of Catco, who lived in the apartment building where her father was the assistant superintendent.
At age 7, she convinced Spector to remove a beauty mark from the cheek of a dinosaur-shaped pillow doll called Pillokins, because she said it looked like a pimple.

At 14 she became Catco's unofficial toy tester and in 1989 became the youngest corporate vice-president in the United States. But with youth came a few problems. She had trouble getting into the annual Toy Fair trade show because at the time she was under the minimum age of 18.
